title: Machine Learning Model Evaluation & Drift Detection
description: A comprehensive reference course covering classification, regression, and ranking metrics, alongside Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) testing and Population Stability Index (PSI) drift monitoring in MLOps.
body: Maintain production machine learning reliability. Master offline model evaluation metrics, ranking metrics (NDCG, MAP), and automated statistical drift detection pipelines.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: Precision vs. Recall Trade-Offs & F1 Score
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A 99% Accurate Fraud Model That's Useless
A team ships a fraud-detection model that reports 99.4% accuracy on a dataset where only 0.5% of transactions are actually fraudulent. Leadership is thrilled — until someone points out that a model which predicts "NOT FRAUD" for every single transaction, with no intelligence at all, would score 99.5% accuracy on that same dataset. Accuracy alone was hiding a model that catches almost no fraud.

### Cost Asymmetry: Choosing the Right Metric

Different mistakes cost different amounts, and the right metric depends entirely on which mistake is worse for the business:

```text
                    Predicted: FRAUD        Predicted: NOT FRAUD
  Actual: FRAUD    │  True Positive (TP)  │  False Negative (FN)  │
                    │  caught the fraud     │  fraud slipped through │
  ──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  Actual: NOT FRAUD │  False Positive (FP)  │  True Negative (TN)    │
                    │  blocked a real user  │  correctly cleared     │
```

```python
def precision(tp: int, fp: int) -> float:
    """Of everything we FLAGGED, what fraction was actually fraud?"""
    return tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) else 0.0

def recall(tp: int, fn: int) -> float:
    """Of everything that WAS fraud, what fraction did we catch?"""
    return tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) else 0.0

def f1_score(tp: int, fp: int, fn: int) -> float:
    """Harmonic mean — punishes models that sacrifice one metric
    entirely to inflate the other (unlike an arithmetic mean)."""
    p, r = precision(tp, fp), recall(tp, fn)
    return 2 * (p * r) / (p + r) if (p + r) else 0.0

# The "always predict NOT FRAUD" model on 10,000 transactions, 50 of
# which are actually fraud:
print(precision(tp=0, fp=0))   # undefined/0.0 — it never flags anything
print(recall(tp=0, fn=50))     # 0.0 — it catches ZERO of the 50 real frauds
# Its accuracy was 99.5%. Its recall — the metric that actually matters
# for "are we catching fraud" — is 0%.
```

| Metric | Formula | Optimize for this when... |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Precision** | TP / (TP + FP) | False positives are expensive (e.g. spam filter blocking a real email) |
| **Recall** | TP / (TP + FN) | False negatives are expensive (e.g. missing a real cancer diagnosis or a real security breach) |
| **F1 Score** | 2·P·R / (P+R) | You need a single balanced number and neither error type dominates |

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Accuracy is only a meaningful metric when classes are roughly balanced. On imbalanced data (fraud, disease screening, security threats — anywhere the positive class is rare), a trivial always-predict-majority-class model can post a deceptively high accuracy while providing zero actual value. Precision and recall, examined together, expose that immediately.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Recommendation & Search Ranking Metrics (NDCG & MAP)
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: The Right Products, the Wrong Order
An e-commerce search model returns all 5 genuinely relevant products for a query — but buries the most relevant one at rank #5, below four barely-relevant results. Precision and recall, which only measure WHICH items were returned (not their order), would score this ranking identically to a perfect one. That's a real gap: users rarely scroll past the first few results, so position matters enormously for search and recommendation quality.

### Measuring Position, Not Just Presence

**Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG)** explicitly penalizes relevant items placed lower in a ranked list by discounting their contribution logarithmically with position:

```python
import numpy as np

def dcg_at_k(relevance_scores: list[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Discounted Cumulative Gain: relevant items ranked lower contribute
    less, discounted by log2(position + 1)."""
    scores = np.asarray(relevance_scores)[:k]
    discounts = np.log2(np.arange(2, len(scores) + 2))
    return float(np.sum(scores / discounts))

def ndcg_at_k(relevance_scores: list[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Normalize DCG against the IDEAL ordering (same items, sorted
    best-first) so the score is comparable across queries with
    different numbers of relevant results."""
    actual = dcg_at_k(relevance_scores, k)
    ideal = dcg_at_k(sorted(relevance_scores, reverse=True), k)
    return actual / ideal if ideal > 0 else 0.0

# Scenario: relevance scores 0-3, in the ORDER the model actually returned them
model_ranking = [0, 1, 1, 0, 3]   # the most relevant item (3) buried at rank 5
ideal_ranking = [3, 1, 1, 0, 0]   # same items, best-first

print(f"NDCG@5: {ndcg_at_k(model_ranking, 5):.3f}")   # ~0.62 — penalized
print(f"NDCG@5: {ndcg_at_k(ideal_ranking, 5):.3f}")    # 1.000 — perfect ordering
```

**Mean Average Precision (MAP)** takes a complementary view for binary relevance (relevant/not relevant, no graded scale): it averages precision computed at every point a relevant item appears, rewarding models that front-load relevant results.

```text
  Query results, ranked 1→5:     [✓ relevant] [✗] [✓ relevant] [✗] [✗]

  Precision@1 = 1/1 = 1.00   (computed only at rank 1, a relevant hit)
  Precision@3 = 2/3 = 0.67   (computed only at rank 3, a relevant hit)

  Average Precision = (1.00 + 0.67) / 2 = 0.835
  MAP = mean of Average Precision across ALL queries in the evaluation set
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: NDCG and MAP both answer a question precision/recall structurally cannot: not just "did we return the right items" but "did we return them in the right ORDER." For any search, recommendation, or ranked-feed system, evaluating on precision/recall alone can mask a model that's technically correct but practically unusable because the good results are buried below the fold.

sections.title: Section 2: Detecting Production Data Drift & Concept Drift

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Data Drift (Covariate Shift) vs. Concept Drift
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Model That Was Never Wrong, Until It Was
A credit-approval model trained on 2023 applicant data performs beautifully in offline evaluation and for the first six months in production. Then approval accuracy quietly degrades. Nobody changed the model. What changed is the WORLD the model is scoring: a new applicant demographic started using the product, and separately, a macroeconomic shift changed what "creditworthy" actually means. These are two distinct failure modes with different fixes.

### Two Kinds of Shift

```text
  DATA DRIFT (covariate shift)              CONCEPT DRIFT
  ─────────────────────────────             ─────────────────────────────
  P(X) changes                               P(Y|X) changes
  Input feature DISTRIBUTION shifts          The relationship between
  the relationship P(Y|X) stays the same     inputs and outcome shifts

  Example: applicant age distribution        Example: a $50k income used
  skews younger post-launch — the model      to reliably predict approval;
  still scores age→creditworthiness          after a recession, $50k no
  correctly, it's just seeing more of a      longer means the same thing
  segment it saw less of during training     about repayment risk

  Fix: retrain on more representative        Fix: the model's LEARNED
  data, or reweight training samples         relationship is now stale —
                                              retraining alone may not be
                                              enough; the labeling logic or
                                              feature set may need revision
```

The distinction matters operationally: data drift is often survivable with routine retraining on fresh data, while concept drift means the model's fundamental assumptions about the world have broken, and simply feeding it more recent data trained the same way may not fix it — the underlying labeling function itself needs re-examination.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: When production accuracy degrades, the very first diagnostic question is: has the INPUT distribution shifted (data drift), or has the INPUT-TO-OUTPUT relationship shifted (concept drift)? Confusing the two leads teams to retrain endlessly against concept drift when the real fix is revisiting labels or features.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Python Implementation: Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) & PSI
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Catching Drift Before It Costs Money
Waiting for accuracy metrics to visibly degrade means you've already been making bad predictions for weeks — accuracy is a lagging indicator that requires ground-truth labels, which for something like loan default might not arrive for months. Statistical drift tests on the INPUT features, by contrast, can run daily with no labels required at all.

### Automated Drift Monitoring: KS Test & PSI

The **Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test** compares two samples' cumulative distributions and returns a p-value indicating whether they plausibly come from the same underlying distribution:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

def detect_ks_drift(reference_data: np.ndarray, current_data: np.ndarray, threshold: float = 0.05) -> bool:
    """Returns True if current_data has likely drifted from the
    reference (training-time) distribution."""
    statistic, p_value = ks_2samp(reference_data, current_data)
    return p_value < threshold

# reference: applicant income at training time
# current: applicant income over the last 7 days in production
training_income = np.random.normal(loc=55000, scale=15000, size=5000)
recent_income = np.random.normal(loc=71000, scale=15000, size=500)  # shifted!

if detect_ks_drift(training_income, recent_income):
    print("ALERT: income distribution has drifted from training data")
```

The **Population Stability Index (PSI)** buckets a feature into bins and measures how much the proportion of observations in each bin has shifted — it's the industry-standard metric in credit risk and finance specifically because, unlike a KS p-value, it gives an interpretable severity scale:

```python
import numpy as np

def calculate_psi(reference: np.ndarray, current: np.ndarray, buckets: int = 10) -> float:
    breakpoints = np.percentile(reference, np.linspace(0, 100, buckets + 1))
    breakpoints[0], breakpoints[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf

    ref_counts, _ = np.histogram(reference, bins=breakpoints)
    cur_counts, _ = np.histogram(current, bins=breakpoints)

    ref_pct = np.clip(ref_counts / len(reference), 1e-4, None)  # avoid log(0)
    cur_pct = np.clip(cur_counts / len(current), 1e-4, None)

    return float(np.sum((cur_pct - ref_pct) * np.log(cur_pct / ref_pct)))

psi = calculate_psi(training_income, recent_income)
print(f"PSI: {psi:.4f}")
# PSI < 0.1  → no significant shift, no action needed
# 0.1 - 0.25 → moderate shift, investigate and monitor closely
# PSI > 0.25 → major shift, retrain or re-evaluate the model urgently
```

```text
  Daily monitoring pipeline (no ground-truth labels required):

  Production traffic ──► Feature extraction ──► calculate_psi() per feature
                                                        │
                                            ┌───────────┼───────────┐
                                            ▼           ▼           ▼
                                       PSI < 0.1   0.1-0.25 PSI   PSI > 0.25
                                       (log only)  (alert on-call) (page + auto
                                                                    retrain trigger)
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: KS and PSI monitor the INPUT features, which means they can fire an alert days or weeks before enough ground-truth outcomes (e.g. loan defaults, churn events) arrive to compute a degraded accuracy metric. This is why production ML systems run both: drift detection as an early warning system, and accuracy/business metrics as the lagging confirmation.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Knowledge Check — Model Evaluation & Drift
lessons.body:
**Question 1:** Why was 99.4% accuracy a misleading metric for the fraud-detection model in Lesson 1.1?

A) Accuracy is never a valid metric for any classification model
B) The dataset was highly imbalanced (0.5% fraud) — a trivial model that always predicts "NOT FRAUD" would also score ~99.5% accuracy while catching zero real fraud, so accuracy alone couldn't distinguish a useless model from a genuinely good one
C) The model's precision was actually 100%
D) Accuracy should have been measured on the training set instead

**Correct answer: B.** On imbalanced classes, accuracy is dominated by the majority class. Precision and especially recall expose what accuracy hides.

---

**Question 2:** Why can two rankings with identical precision and recall have very different NDCG scores?

A) NDCG and precision/recall measure completely unrelated things with no relationship
B) Precision and recall only measure WHICH items were returned, not the ORDER they appear in — NDCG explicitly discounts relevant items that appear lower in the ranked list, so burying the best result at rank 5 scores worse under NDCG even though the same 5 relevant items were returned either way
C) NDCG is just precision multiplied by recall
D) NDCG can only be computed for binary relevance, unlike precision/recall

**Correct answer: B.** NDCG captures ranking QUALITY (position-sensitive), which is orthogonal to precision/recall's ranking-agnostic "were the right items present at all."

---

**Question 3:** Why do teams run KS/PSI drift monitoring on input features in ADDITION to tracking model accuracy in production?

A) KS and PSI are more accurate than direct accuracy measurement
B) Accuracy requires ground-truth labels, which for something like loan defaults may take months to arrive — KS and PSI monitor the input feature distribution directly and need no labels at all, so they can surface a warning days or weeks before enough outcomes exist to compute a degraded accuracy number
C) PSI replaces the need for any accuracy tracking
D) KS and PSI are only useful for detecting concept drift, not data drift

**Correct answer: B.** Input-distribution drift tests are a leading indicator that requires no ground truth; accuracy-based monitoring is a lagging indicator that confirms the business impact once labels arrive.
